settings.editor: What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Pain along the arch or where it meets the heel
  • Worst with the first steps of the day
  • Eases with movement, then returns after rest
  • Sore to press along the inside of the arch

Pronation elongates the plantar fascia. As the foot rolls in and the arch drops, the fascia is stretched on every step, and that repeated stretching causes micro-tears at the base of the heel, where it attaches. How much load it takes, and from which direction, depends on foot alignment, a change in activity or footwear, and the way the leg above is working.

image.alt: Diagram of the plantar fascia showing inflammation and tearing

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of the plantar fascia showing inflammation and tearing</figcaption>
In detail
The plantar fascia is a band of tissue running from the heel bone to the ball of the foot. Plantar fasciitis is what happens when it is repeatedly over-stretched at its attachment on the heel.

image.alt: Pain highlighted under the heel where the plantar fascia attaches

settings.editor: How it progresses
Early
Constant, repetitive strain causes tiny tears and inflammation where the fascia attaches to the heel.
Longer term
The body lays down thickening and scar tissue. There is usually no longer inflammation, and it becomes harder to treat.
Compensation
A small bony growth forms at the attachment.
01

When the foot rolls in too far, the arch drops and the foot lengthens. That stretches the fascia at its heel attachment on every step. Overnight it is not under load, which is why getting out of bed hurts most.
02
The fascia has inner, central and outer bands. Inner heel pain is linked with rolling in, outer heel pain with rolling out, and centre heel pain with both.
03
If one leg is longer, that foot may roll in more to level the body up, straining the inner heel. The plan can then include raising the shorter leg, not just supporting the arch.
04
Orthotics and additions, strapping, massage and foot adjustments, shockwave, dry needling and injection therapy.
How we diagnose it
Plantar Fasciitis is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We look at how the arch loads when you walk rather than only at rest, because the fascia is loaded as you move.
02
We identify what is increasing that load and explain what we found before anything is prescribed.
03
Treatment is matched to the finding, which is why the plan differs between two people with the same diagnosis.

Questions

settings.title: Is plantar fasciitis the same as heel pain?

settings.editor: They overlap. Heel pain is the symptom; plantar fasciitis is one of the common causes of it.

Stretching is often suggested, but where the fascia is already over-stretched and tearing, pulling on it can tear it further. Your podiatrist will tell you whether stretching has any place in your plan, and what to do instead.
That depends on how long it has been there. You will get a realistic timeframe at the assessment rather than a standard answer.
Usually not. The diagnosis is made from the assessment. Imaging is requested only where it would change the plan.
